title: Shared input predicts functional coupling beyond direct wiring, distance and node effects in 40 worms, 49 flies and 79 anesthetized mice; the best polysynaptic measure is different in each animal
abstract: Question: does polysynaptic structure predict pairwise functional connectivity (FC) beyond the direct connection, and does one rule apply in different animals? Data (all from earlier campaign work): C. elegans whole-brain calcium imaging (40 animals, 134 identified neurons) with the Cook 2019 connectome; Drosophila light-field imaging (50 flies, 75 neuropils) with FlyWire v783 neuron-mediated region flow; mouse resting fMRI (79 mice, medetomidine + isoflurane, 304 isocortex parcels) with the Knox 2019 tracer model. Method: for each pair we computed the direct weight and four polysynaptic measures: shared input (SI), shared output, two-step relay and communicability. In each individual we regressed Fisher-z FC on node fixed effects, distance terms, homologous pair, node-strength product, the direct terms and each measure. Inference used individuals, node-permutation (DSP-QAP) tests on group FC, distance-bin weight shuffles and, in the worm, degree-preserving rewiring. Results: SI predicted FC beyond the direct connection in each animal (pre-specified H1 supported): mean partial r 0.053 (39 of 40 worms), 0.077 (45 of 49 flies), 0.133 (79 of 79 mice); group partial r 0.074, 0.235, 0.196 (QAP p = 0.001), above all randomised-wiring surrogates, and still positive after control for the same measures on a pure distance graph. SI was the only measure with a positive unique effect in the joint model in all three animals. The rank order of the four measures differed between animals (H3 not supported). Indirect terms added more unique variance than direct terms in the fly (0.69 vs 0.09 %) and mouse (1.46 vs 0.65 %), but not in the worm (0.57 vs 0.50 %). All unique gains are small. The SI effect repeated in rest and walk (fly), behaviour-removed traces (worm) and isoflurane-only mice, but it was weak in 6 awake mice. Limitations: connectomes and activity come from different individuals; the mouse graph lacks subcortical paths and is spatially smoothed; dense graphs make direct and indirect measures highly collinear; QAP ignores spatial autocorrelation.
